उत्तर में फिर से भारी बारिश, मध्य क्षेत्र में भीषण गर्मी।
(डैन ट्राई अखबार) - 26 अगस्त को उत्तरी क्षेत्र में गरज के साथ भारी बारिश होने का अनुमान है, जिसमें कुछ क्षेत्रों में 80 मिमी से अधिक बारिश हो सकती है; जबकि दक्षिण मध्य तट पर भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में तापमान 38 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक हो सकता है।
Báo Dân trí•25/08/2026
राष्ट्रीय जल-मौसम विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, 26 अगस्त को उत्तरी वियतनाम और थान्ह होआ प्रांत में छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ बारिश होगी, जिसमें आमतौर पर 15-30 मिमी बारिश होगी और कुछ स्थानों पर 80 मिमी से अधिक भारी बारिश भी हो सकती है।
मौसम विज्ञान एजेंसी ने चेतावनी दी है कि गरज के साथ आने वाले तूफान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवा के झोंके ला सकते हैं।
मौसम की ये खतरनाक घटनाएं कृषि उत्पादन को प्रभावित कर सकती हैं, पेड़ों को गिरा सकती हैं और घरों, परिवहन बुनियादी ढांचे और अन्य सुविधाओं को नुकसान पहुंचा सकती हैं।
गौरतलब है कि कम समय में होने वाली स्थानीय भारी वर्षा से छोटी नदियों और नालों में अचानक बाढ़ आ सकती है, ढलानों पर भूस्खलन हो सकता है और निचले इलाकों में जलभराव हो सकता है।
मध्य क्षेत्र में, 26-27 अगस्त को, ह्यू से दा नांग तक का क्षेत्र, क्वांग न्गाई से डाक लक और खान्ह होआ प्रांतों के पूर्वी हिस्से गर्म मौसम का अनुभव करेंगे, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ेगी और अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा, और कुछ स्थानों पर 38 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है; न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 45-50% रहेगी।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
26 अगस्त के लिए देश भर का मौसम पूर्वानुमान:
हनोई : आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे, बीच-बीच में हल्की बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है। उत्तर-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवा चलेगी। तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की आशंका है। न्यूनतम तापमान 25-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस; अधिकतम तापमान 31-33 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
उत्तर-पश्चिमी क्षेत्र: बादल छाए रहेंगे, छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी बारिश हो सकती है। हवा हल्की रहेगी। गरज के साथ बौछारों के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है। न्यूनतम तापमान 23-26 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ स्थानों पर 22 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे भी जा सकता है; अधिकतम तापमान 30-33 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ स्थानों पर 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस से ऊपर भी जा सकता है।
पूर्वोत्तर वियतनाम: आसमान में बादल छाए रहेंगे, छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, कुछ इलाकों में भारी बारिश हो सकती है। उत्तर से उत्तर-पश्चिम दिशा की ओर 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ बौछारों के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है। न्यूनतम तापमान 24-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, पहाड़ी इलाकों में 23 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे; अधिकतम तापमान 30-33 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा।
थान्ह होआ - ह्यू : शाम और रात में बादल छाए रहेंगे, छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है; दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी, कुछ इलाकों में गर्मी रहेगी। पश्चिम से दक्षिण-पश्चिम की ओर 2-3 ब्यूफोर्ट की गति से हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है। न्यूनतम तापमान 25-28 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा। उत्तर में अधिकतम तापमान 28-31 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा; दक्षिण में 32-35 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ इलाकों में तापमान 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है।
दक्षिण मध्य तट: शाम और रात में बादल छाए रहेंगे और छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आने की संभावना है; दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी और गर्मी रहेगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ सकती है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवा के झोंके आने की संभावना है। न्यूनतम तापमान 26-29 डिग्री सेल्सियस; अधिकतम तापमान 34-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में तापमान 38 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक हो सकता है।

Japan’s ‘2050 Weather Forecast’ highlights extreme heat in the future
As extreme heat becomes an increasingly visible reality across Japan, meteorologists, scientists, businesses and professional footballers are joining forces to encourage stronger climate action and raise awareness of the risks posed by global warming.
A newly updated climate awareness initiative in Japan is drawing attention to what life could look like in 2050 if greenhouse gas emissions continue their current trajectory.
The initiative, which has as its centerpiece the 2050 Weather Forecast video, comes as Japan grapples with increasingly severe heat.
The newly introduced term kokushobi, or “extreme heat day”, describes days when temperatures reach 40°C or higher.
Such conditions have regularly dominated national headlines, while reports that three lions died from heat stroke at a Tokyo Zoo have further highlighted the growing
impacts of rising temperatures.
When tomorrow arrives ahead of schedule
The new video updates an earlier forecast produced by Japan’s national broadcaster, NHK, in 2014 as part of a campaign by the UN’s World Meteorological Organization (WMO) which dramatically highlights how weather reports in 2050 will be characterized by extreme heat.
Featuring the same weather forecaster and climate scientist, the latest version reflects both accelerating global warming and the latest scientific analysis.
Several scenarios presented in the 2014 forecast have already become reality years earlier than anticipated. Among them are prolonged periods of temperatures exceeding 35°C, once presented as a potential future outcome for mid-century Japan.
The updated forecast imagines conditions in 2050 under current climate policies.
It projects that "extreme heat days" could be recorded in as many as 157 locations across the country.
Measures to protect public health could include restrictions on outdoor activities, preventing children from playing outside and construction workers from carrying out work in open-air conditions.
The video also warns of mounting pressures on food production and daily life. One example suggests that a popular Japanese pork cutlet rice dish could become a luxury item.
It also highlights the possibility of increasingly destructive "super typhoons" bringing severe damage across the country.
Towards a decarbonized society
At the same time, the forecast points to solutions, including a faster transition to renewable energy and wider adoption of electric vehicles as part of the shift towards a decarbonized society.
The initiative has been supported by the UN in Japan, and the video has been made freely available for public use.
Its release comes amid growing calls for countries to strengthen efforts not only to cut emissions but also to protect communities from climate impacts already being felt today.
"Because even at full speed, we cannot outrun climate change," UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a speech on 28 June.
"Its impacts are already here – compounding and cascading."
Footballers join climate awareness campaign
Professional football players are also helping bring the climate message to new audiences.
Japan's professional football league, the J.LEAGUE, has introduced measures to reduce heat-related risks for both players and spectators, including adjusting match schedules to avoid the hottest parts of the day during increasingly hot and humid summers.
The league has also partnered with the campaign I am one of the 89% who want to stop global warming, promoted jointly by the United Nations and Japanese media organizations.
Six J.LEAGUE Climate Action Ambassadors have recorded video messages for the initiative, including Hiroki Yamada, a long-time star of Júbilo Iwata.
In his message, Mr. Yamada expresses concern that children may increasingly be unable to play outdoors during summer and emphasizes the role individuals can play in addressing climate change.
His message was shown on the giant screen at Júbilo Iwata's opening home match of the 2026/27 season on 8 August. The match kicked off at 7 pm as part of league-wide efforts to reduce heat-related risks.
Organizers hope that reaching football supporters alongside wider audiences will help encourage greater public engagement on climate action at a time when the impacts of rising temperatures are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

South Korea records nearly double average number of heat wave days
As of Monday, the country had experienced 20.1 heat wave days, compared with a long-term average of 10.4 days for the same period, the weather agency said Tuesday.
The KMA issues a heat wave advisory when the maximum apparent temperature is expected to remain above 33 C for at least two consecutive days.
South Korea has endured exceptionally hot weather this summer, with temperatures reaching a record 42.5 C in the southeastern city of Yangsan on Aug. 2. The reading was the highest recorded on the Korean Peninsula since modern weather observations began in 1904.
The country has also experienced 16.4 tropical nights so far this year, the second-highest figure on record after 16.8 nights recorded in 1994. A tropical night occurs when the nighttime temperature remains at or above 25 C.
The KMA expects the hot weather to continue into next month, attributing the prolonged heat to a “double heat dome” caused by strengthening North Pacific and Tibetan high-pressure systems over the Korean Peninsula.
Earlier, Qazinform reported the global average sea surface temperature had reached its highest daily level on record, with the latest reading exceeding the previous record set in March 2024.

A new heatwave is on its way to central and southern Italy; it is set to be the most intense of the summer
The number of ‘red alerts’ is on the rise: on Thursday 27 August, there will be three – in Bari, Campobasso and Palermo. Cooler weather is expected in the northern regions
A new heatwave – the fifth of the year – is set to hit the country. The heatwave won’t last long (the situation could improve as early as the second half of the weekend) but it will be particularly intense in central and southern Italy, where it is forecast to be the most severe of the entire season, with temperatures peaking well above 40 degrees. “The worst days,” explains Lorenzo Tedici, head meteorologist at iLMeteo.it, “will be Thursday 27th, Friday 28th and Saturday 29th” August. The northern part of the peninsula, where further showers and thunderstorms are expected, will largely be spared, maintaining a cooler and more comfortable climate.
The red stickers
The number of red alerts is on the rise again. Following a brief lull around mid-August, the highest alert level has returned in some municipalities – particularly in the south and on the islands – indicating emergency conditions with potential adverse effects even on the health of healthy, active people, and not just on those in at-risk groups.
On Wednesday 26 August, Campobasso and Palermo will be on ‘red’ alert, with Bari joining them the following day. The number of ‘orange’ alerts is also rising: nine are forecast for Thursday 27 August, in Ancona, Cagliari, Catania, Florence, Latina, Messina, Reggio Calabria, Rieti and Rome, confirming that the situation is most critical in central and southern Italy.
Consequently, the number of urban centres where the minimum alert level remains in place is falling. On Thursday, only six of the 27 municipalities monitored by the Ministry of Health in its daily heatwave bulletin will remain ‘in the green’. Most of these regional capitals are located in the north of the country, with the exception of Frosinone; they are Milan, Genoa, Turin, Trieste and Venice.
The New Wave
In central and southern Italy, therefore, the subtropical high-pressure system that has brought extreme temperatures throughout the summer does not appear set to retreat any time soon. According to forecasts from iLMeteo.it, the intense heat is set to return from Thursday 27 August: ‘A deep trough is approaching from Northern Europe, set to move towards the ocean off the coast of Portugal. This will create the conditions for a surge of very hot air from North Africa, heading straight for the Mediterranean and Italia.’

Newswise — Green and blue spaces, such as woodlands and riversides, could provide a vital line of defence for cities facing increasingly hot summers, according to new research from the University of Surrey.
In a study published in Environment International, leading researchers from Surrey’s Global Centre for Clean Air Research (GCARE) monitored temperatures across Guildford for three years to understand how different urban environments cope with heat. The team compared six types of green and blue infrastructure – woodland, lakeside, grassland, a pocket park, riverside and a green wall. They then compared temperatures with a built-up area between June 2023 and August 2025.
During peak summer hours, all six of the green and blue sites were cooler than the built-up location. The woodland site recorded the greatest difference, at around 2.5°C cooler, followed by grassland at 2.3°C and lakeside at 2.1°C.
Across ten extreme heat events that were analysed during the study, the woodland site was on average 4.5°C cooler during the daytime than the built-up site, with differences frequently exceeding 5-6°C during the most severe heatwaves. Grassland and lakeside were around 4°C cooler on average.
Researchers also compared how often each location experienced heatwave conditions, defined in Surrey as temperatures reaching at least 28°C for three consecutive days. Over the three summers, the built-up site experienced 54 heatwave days, with heatwave conditions accounting for 19.6 per cent of summer daytime observations. In comparison, all six green and blue spaces experienced significantly less extreme heat. The green wall recorded the highest exposure of the six at 8.7 per cent, while the woodland area recorded no heatwave periods at all.
Professor Prashant Kumar, Founding Director of GCARE at the University of Surrey and corresponding author of the study, said:
“Summer 2026 has felt like a wake-up call for the impact of increasingly hot summers, and we now have three years of evidence showing the difference nature can make. What was most surprising was the woodland site, where we recorded no heatwave conditions – compared with almost a fifth of summer daytime observations at the built-up location.
“There is no one-size-fits-all solution, but our findings show why trees, green spaces and water should be an important part of how we design towns and cities to cope with a warmer climate.”
As part of GCARE’s Guildford Living Lab, the study used a network of sensors to record temperature and humidity every minute at the seven locations across Guildford over three years, alongside satellite data to provide a broader picture of urban temperatures. Satellite observations also showed substantial differences in summer surface temperatures, particularly between the built-up, woodland and lakeside areas.
While woodland showed some of the largest and most consistent temperature differences, the research team cautions that each type of green and blue infrastructure was represented by one location, meaning local conditions may have influenced the results. Future studies could examine multiple examples of each type and how their cooling effects extend into surrounding streets and neighbourhoods.
Soheila Khalili, postgraduate researcher at GCARE and lead author of the study, said:
“After three years of monitoring these sites through ordinary summer days and intense heatwaves, it was striking to see just how differently they responded to the same conditions. As our summers get hotter, this kind of long-term evidence can help us make better decisions about the green and blue spaces we build into our towns and cities.”
The work was supported through RECLAIM Network Plus, GP4Streets, GreenCities, GREENIN and University Global Partnership Network-funded projects.
Reference:
Khalili, S., Jones, L., & Kumar, P. (2026). Microclimatic performance of greening against urban overheating: a multiseasonal analysis using in-situ monitoring and satellite data. Environment International 215, 110452. Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envint.2026.110452
[ENDS]

articles.title: Extreme heat becomes dangerous much sooner as the human body ages - Earth.com

articles.full_text:
Extreme heat becomes dangerous much sooner as the human body ages
Older adults can reach dangerous heat limits much sooner than younger people, putting millions at risk as global temperatures continue to rise.
Extreme heat becomes dangerous when the body can no longer cool itself properly.
Sweating helps cool the body as moisture evaporates from the skin, but high humidity makes this harder, and older adults may have more difficulty staying cool.
Physiologists call the point beyond which internal body temperature cannot stay steady “uncompensable heat stress.”
After that limit is crossed, body temperature keeps rising, increasing the danger of heat illness and worsening heart, lung, or kidney problems.
A new global projection suggests earlier estimates may have missed how much danger older adults face.
When researchers used heat limits for different age groups, they found much greater risk for people aged 60 and older.
Older adults struggle more with heat
Older adults often sweat less, send less blood toward the skin, and have less ability to increase how much blood the heart pumps during heat.
As a result, cooling can fail at lower combinations of temperature and humidity.
Dr. Qinqin Kong, a postdoctoral scholar at Stanford Health Policy, led the analysis.
“The human body can tolerate only a limited range of ambient heat,” Dr. Kong said.
“Understanding where, when, and to what extent these limits are exceeded is critical for informing climate prevention policies.”
Models show heat risk by age
The team used laboratory data from 52 young adults, 26 middle-aged adults, and 55 older adults.
In chambers, researchers raised heat or humidity while monitoring internal body temperature and heart rate.
They identified the combinations where body temperature began rising continuously, then combined those age-based limits with 14 computer climate models and population projections for people 15 and older.
The analysis examined warming from 1.8°F to 7.2°F above preindustrial temperatures and used wet-bulb temperature.
This is a measure that combines heat and humidity to help gauge the body’s ability to cool through sweating.
Professor Eran Bendavid of the Stanford School of Medicine was a senior author of the study.
“As the planet warms, it is critical to understand where, when, and to what extent environmental conditions will exceed human heat tolerance,” Professor Bendavid said.
Older adults face dangerous heat sooner
At just 2.7°F (1.5°C) of global warming, older adults faced dangerous heat more often and across more places than young adults did at 7.2°F (4°C) of warming.
When researchers used heat limits for each age group, the number of people exposed was 8.2 times higher at 2.7°F of warming and twice as high at 7.2°F.
At 2.7°F of warming, about 290 million older adults were projected to face dangerous heat for at least 180 hours each year. That is equivalent to about six hours a day for one month.
For every extra 1.8°F (1°C) of warming, about 1 billion more people could face this level of heat.
At 5.4°F of warming, around 2 billion people aged 15 and older were projected to be exposed, including 1.3 billion older adults.
“Our results suggest accounting for age-stratified vulnerability, intolerable heat will be experienced at much larger scales and for longer durations,” Dr. Kong said.
Dangerous heat hits some countries hardest
At 5.4°F of warming, India, China, Pakistan, and Bangladesh together accounted for about 1.48 billion exposed people.
That was nearly three-quarters of everyone projected to face at least 180 hours beyond their age-specific limit.
Exposure reached 100 percent in Bahrain and Qatar, while the United Arab Emirates reached nearly 95 percent.
The entire older population was projected to face this level in seven countries.
“The projected concentration of risk in tropical and subtropical regions poses severe challenges for energy reliability, grid resilience, and access to cooling, particularly in low- and middle-income countries with limited adaptive capacity,” Dr. Kong said.
Adaptive capacity means having the resources and support needed to prepare for extreme heat and keep people safe.
Heat can persist overnight
The dangerous conditions were often packed into the hottest months.
For older adults in Delhi, Lahore, and Dubai, the models projected close to or more than 1,000 hours beyond the limit at 2.7°F of warming, rising above 2,000 hours at 5.4°F.
At higher warming levels, some places faced repeated exposure during both day and night for several months.
Fewer resources make heat hard to manage
The team used poverty rates as a rough measure of countries’ ability to respond, but this cannot capture power access, health care, or housing.
At 5.4°F of warming, 13 countries had poverty rates above 50 percent and either at least 10 million exposed older adults or at least 80 percent of their older population exposed.
India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and Niger met both exposure measures. The paper points to stronger warnings, reliable electricity, cooling centers, safer indoor spaces, and prepared health services.
“Our findings indicate that intolerable heat will affect far more people, across larger regions, and for longer periods than previously recognized,” Dr. Kong and Professor Bendavid wrote.
“By identifying which age groups are exposed, and where, and at which warming levels, our findings can inform targeted heat action plans, emergency preparedness, and health system planning.”
Limitations of the study
These results describe possible futures from computer models, not certain outcomes.
The heat limits came mainly from people who were not accustomed to tropical heat, so the analysis may overestimate exposure in hot regions.
A test that adjusted the limits for local climate reduced projected exposure, but the main pattern remained. Older adults still carried a larger burden than younger groups.
Other choices may push the estimates too low.
Broad climate models cannot fully capture hotter city neighborhoods, poorly ventilated homes, informal settlements, heavy outdoor labor, or health strain that begins before body temperature rises continuously.
The middle-aged limit required some estimation because that group completed fewer laboratory tests, although another method produced similar results.
The country comparison also assumed that poverty patterns would stay similar.
Protecting older adults from extreme heat
The analysis shows that warming alone does not determine who faces intolerable heat.
The age of a population can greatly change how many people face dangerous heat, when it happens, and where the risk is highest.
That makes protecting older adults a central part of planning for extreme heat.
Cutting future warming would reduce exposure, but many older adults may face dangerous conditions even at lower warming levels.
Heat plans also need to improve housing, cooling access, power reliability, warnings, and medical response.
The study is published in the journal The Lancet Planetary Health.

Press releases are posted on Independent.com as a free community service.
The County of Santa Barbara Health Department (County Health) is issuing a Health Alert due to the Extreme Heat Warning issued by the National Weather Service for parts of Santa Barbara County. The National Weather Service is forecasting continued hot and dry weather with elevated fire conditions, through at least Friday with major heat risk on Tuesday for most areas including most coastal sections and concerns for heat-related illness.
A Heat Advisory is in effect until 10:00 a.m. Tuesday, August 25th with temperatures up to 107 expected.
An Extreme Heat Watch will be in effect from Tuesday morning, August 25th through Friday evening, August 28th with dangerously hot conditions expected and temperatures up to 112 possible.
County Health is urging residents to take the necessary safety measures to avoid heat- related illnesses, including heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Community members are strongly encouraged to take the following precautions whenever temperatures are on the rise:
- Take care of those who might not be aware of the danger or be able to react accordingly – especially the elderly, young children, and pets. Check on your neighbors.
- Wear appropriate clothing. Lightweight, light-colored, loose fitting clothing works best.
- Drink plenty of cool, non-alcoholic beverages, especially those without sugar or caffeine. Do not wait until you are thirsty to drink. If you have fluid restrictions from your doctor, ask to see how much you should drink while the weather is hot.
- Limit outdoor activity. Try to schedule outdoor activities during the cooler parts of the day, like morning and evening hours. Be sure to wear sunscreen and rest often.
- Take regular breaks in the shade or in an air-conditioned room. A few hours in air conditioning can help your body stay cooler. Taking a cool shower or bath can help too.
- If you do not have air‐conditioning, consider arranging to spend at least parts of the day at another space that is cool. Electric fans may provide comfort, but when the temperature is in the high 90s, they will not prevent heat-related illness.
- For those who work outside, be sure to take frequent rest breaks in a shaded area or air-conditioned room, if possible. Stay hydrated and take action by moving to a cooler space if you feel signs of heat exhaustion.
- Know the signs of heat exhaustion. If someone becomes dizzy, nauseated, or sweats heavily, find a cooler location for him or her immediately.
- Know the signs of heat stroke. Heat stroke is much more serious than heat exhaustion. The symptoms are similar to heat exhaustion, but also include hot, flushed skin. With heat stroke, the person often stops sweating and the skin will be unusually dry. If heat stroke is a possibility, call 911 immediately. Heat stroke is life threatening!
- Do not leave children (or pets) unattended in vehicles. It only takes a matter of minutes on a relatively mild day for a vehicle to reach deadly temperatures.
Make a plan to keep cool during the hot weather days ahead and don’t forget to include your pets in the plan. Pets, just like humans, are susceptible to the dangerous effects of extreme heat. Visit CDPH’s website: Protecting Your Pet During Hot Weather for steps you can take to ensure the well-being of your pets during this heat wave. For more information about the extreme heat forecast, visit: Heatwave and Fire Weather in SBC | Santa Barbara County, CA – Official Website.

articles.title: Japanese farmers go nocturnal as extreme heat makes days more dangerous - The Globe and Mail
articles.search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
articles.full_text:
Long after sunset, Motoaki Iijima’s illuminated greenhouse north of Tokyo glows like a lantern as the flower farmer harvests pink and orange gerberas, avoiding a daytime sun fierce enough to be deadly.
As increasingly intense heat waves turn Japanese summers into survival tests, farmers – from flower and asparagus growers to egg producers – are rewriting the agrarian clock. Once-busy midday hours are now avoided as a mortal threat, replaced by after-dark work to protect crops, livestock and themselves.
Mr. Iijima, 36, converted his family’s centuries-old rice farm in the rural town of Nikko into a flower farm a decade ago. Three summers ago, after a part-time worker suffered heatstroke picking sunflowers in his greenhouse, he made a dramatic change. Outside temperatures above 35 degrees – increasingly common in his region – can push greenhouse interiors above 40. Now, Mr. Iijima works outdoors through the night, stopping only when the morning sun turns punishing again.
From rice farmers in Vietnam to winery workers in Spain, farmers across the globe are shifting work to cooler nighttime and early-morning hours as they try to beat more frequent and intense heatwaves.
The numbers tell a stark story.
Japan is especially exposed: around 70 per cent of its farmers are 65 or older, a population especially susceptible to heat stress, and high humidity amplifies the danger.
A record 59 agricultural workers succumbed to extreme heat in 2024 in Japan, more than double the death toll in 2021. About 60 per cent of farmers in their 20s to 50s surveyed by Japan Weather Association last year said they had either personally suffered heatstroke or knew someone who had. Nearly 60 per cent of farmers also shifted their working hours to earlier or later in the day.
In 2024 alone, heat exposure cost Japan’s agricultural sector 926 million labour hours – time workers could not safely spend in the fields – according to Lancet Countdown, a research collaboration that tracks the health impacts of climate change. Across all sectors, labour hours lost to heat nearly doubled from the 1990s average, translating to roughly $46-billion in lost income, or about 1 per cent of Japan’s gross domestic product.
To adapt, workers at Mr. Iijima’s farm now start work up to two hours earlier. One veteran worker, 68-year-old Miyoko Asada, arrives at the farm shortly after sunrise.
“We’ve got to race against the clock,” she says, hurrying to cut purple asters alongside eight others in a vast field before temperatures climb past safety limits.
A few towns away, poultry farmer Tetsuya Usuba faces a different crisis. Six summers ago, he lost more than 500 laying hens to heatstroke during a three-day spell of intense heat. The experience still haunts Usuba – he and his father had to use a forklift fitted with a giant bucket to remove the birds from the barn.
Now, Mr. Usuba’s midnight routine is fixed: lights automatically flick on in two of his barns at 2:30 a.m., waking the 4,400 caged hens to eat before oppressive heat suppresses their appetite. He has installed additional fans, sprays water on the barn’s metal roofs, and adds citric acid to the hens’ drinking water. Still, when temperatures suddenly spiked above 35 last month, he lost 130 birds.
“Summer has become a new threat to producers like us, something as scary as an outbreak of avian influenza,” the 48-year-old says. As he checked on his birds one recent afternoon, the thermometer read 33. Many of them were panting with their beaks ajar.
The government has taken note. New workplace regulations introduced in 2025 require employers to establish heatstroke reporting procedures and emergency response plans. Japan is also promoting smart farming technologies such as the use of drones and robots to reduce workers’ heat exposure.
But on Mr. Iijima’s farm, adaptation remains intensely manual. In the early morning, workers hurriedly check the harvested flowers for wilting leaves before loading them onto trucks. It is not yet 8 a.m., and the morning is still bearable. “Look, those leaves are already wilting,” one worker calls out.

In Photos: Heavy rain lashes Delhi-NCR; IMD issues red alert
Heavy rain lashed several parts of Delhi and adjoining areas of the National Capital Region (NCR) on Tuesday morning, disrupting normal life and causing waterlogging in several areas. (Pics/PTI and AFP)
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a district-level red alert covering all 11 districts of Delhi. The warning was valid until 9:45 am.
Persistent showers led to water accumulation on roads and low-lying stretches, raising concerns about traffic disruptions during the morning rush hour.
Heavy showers were reported from prominent locations including Parliament Street, Connaught Place, the AIIMS area, ITO, R.K. Puram and Ferozeshah Road.
The IMD forecast moderate rainfall at many places across Delhi, with isolated locations likely to receive heavy to extremely heavy showers. Thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds are also expected.
The latest weather warning came a day after intense rainfall caused extensive waterlogging, traffic congestion and disruptions to flight operations across Delhi-NCR.
Gurugram and Faridabad were placed under a yellow alert, with further rainfall expected. Noida remained heavily overcast, although no specific weather warning had been issued for the city.
On Monday, heavy rain brought traffic to a crawl across several parts of Delhi, Gurugram and Noida, with long queues reported on major roads as rainwater accumulated on key stretches.
Air travel was also disrupted on Monday, with 26 flights cancelled, 15 diverted to other cities and more than 390 delayed during the day.
The latest spell of rain pushed cumulative monsoon rainfall above normal at several Delhi weather stations. Till August 24, Safdarjung recorded 246.2 mm against a normal of 191.1 mm, an excess of 29 per cent.
Palam received 227.2 mm, 28 per cent above normal, while Lodi Road recorded 233.2 mm, 22 per cent higher than normal. Ridge recorded 243 mm, 50 per cent above normal, while Ayanagar received 266.3 mm, 66 per cent above normal.
The IMD attributed the intense showers to the interaction between a middle- and upper-level western disturbance and a lower-tropospheric trough extending from a low-pressure area over Gangetic West Bengal towards southwest Uttar Pradesh.
Air quality across Delhi-NCR remained largely in the poor category. Anand Vihar recorded the highest pollution level among the listed stations, with an AQI of 208.
AQI readings included Mundka at 81, CRRI Mathura Road at 96, Rohini at 130, Punjabi Bagh at 114, Chandni Chowk at 135, Narela at 90, Shadipur at 64, R.K. Puram at 109, Pusa at 123, North Campus at 131, Cantonment Area at 103 and Sonia Vihar at 131.
